claims.text: A new computational method using ab initio molecular dynamics or density functional theory with advanced potentials can accurately predict lattice heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed method can accurately predict electronic heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr separately from lattice heat transport.
The proposed method will outperform earlier approaches by capturing atomic-scale complexity.
Accounting for defects and impurities will improve heat-transport predictions for HfNbTaTiZr.
The applicable material state is a bulk HfNbTaTiZr crystal that may contain defects and impurities such as 1 wt.% oxygen.
A new interatomic potential can account for defect and impurity effects on lattice heat transport.
A new interatomic potential can account for defect and impurity effects on electronic heat transport.
The method is applicable below 200 K and from 300 to 1200 K.
Lattice distortions are relevant structural features in high-entropy solid-solution alloys.
Lattice distortions and defects mediate heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
Ab initio molecular dynamics combined with machine-learned force fields and Green-Kubo analysis can be used to derive thermal conductivity.
Density functional theory is an effective computational approach for identifying alloy structures and properties.
The proposed method will improve prediction of the separate lattice and electronic heat-transport contributions.
Use of the proposed computational method may increase the total conductivity of the material.
The baseline total conductivity is 10–17 W/(K m) from 300 to 1200 K.
The method's sample applicability includes bulk crystals with defects and impurities.
Predictions should be compared with experiments on HfNbTaTiZr samples having varied defect and impurity concentrations.
The falsification experiment should measure total conductivity and separately resolved lattice and electronic contributions.
A significant deviation between predicted and experimental total conductivity would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention is development of a predictive computational method, but the outcome suggests a potential increase in the material's total conductivity. A modeling intervention can change prediction accuracy but does not itself increase the physical conductivity.

The hypothesis emphasizes separately predicting lattice and electronic contributions, whereas the stated falsification rule relies only on total conductivity and therefore does not decisively test separation of the two channels.
